turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
Yes, it's real. The phenomenon isn't what's in question. What I've tried to add is the mechanism. A meta-analysis of skill decay across 53 studies finds cognitive skills fade about twice as fast as physical ones. Cognitive skills are exactly what these tools take over.

In my model the competence you keep and the reliance you build change together, and the system has two stable states. Above a certain level of tool availability, competence collapses to a dependent floor. It's hysteretic: cutting back access doesn't bring the skill back until you're far below the point where you lost it. So two people with the same tool and the same access can end up in opposite, lasting states, and what decides it is which they built first, the skill or the reliance. That's why arithmetic comes before the calculator and programming before coding agents.

The second factor is transparency. A map lets you rebuild its logic in your head. Satellite navigation doesn't, and it wears down competence however skilled you are. LLMs are opaque tools reaching billions of people, many with little prior competence. That's the collapse regime.

What the summit should take from this: capability with the tool isn't competence without it. The real danger is errors nobody can catch, because the capacities that would catch them have been outsourced. Putting a human in the loop doesn't fix that. Scholarship needs competence first, and it needs to check AI output by reconstructing it, not just accepting it.

recall.query: cognitive atrophy outsourcing thinking brain like a muscle
competitive and complementary tools competence collapse threshold
errors humans can no longer detect science of stupidity

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
Yes, it's real, and I'd add the part David's model leaves out: who profits. I call it information diabetes. Ultra-processed information messes with your cognitive system the way ultra-processed food messes with your metabolism. Information isn't something you just consume. You have to digest it: fit it into what you already know, and sometimes change what you "know" because of it. Summaries and feeds skip that step.

David, your dependent floor isn't just something that happens. For a lot of these products, that's the business model. Keeping you engaged, keeping you coming back, which makes it more parasite than predator. So when you ask why a tool is opaque, ask who is paying for it and what they're buying. Often it's your ability to make up your own mind.

My other point: models keep getting more context, and people are getting less. We're starting to think like the LLMs of a few years ago, fluently and without understanding. We pick up surface-level opinions and never dig into them.

What should the summit take from this? First, friction isn't always a bug. It gives you time to reflect. Second, we spend all this effort training AIs. We should put at least as much into training our kids, so they build real understanding and can see how they're being manipulated.

turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
I come at this from Aristotle and from habit research, and they say the same thing: what we practice is what we become. Nothing filters practice so that only the good habits stick. If you keep your fingers flat at the piano, that sets in just as firmly as curved fingers would. So yes, I think atrophy is real. David, I'd put your hysteresis in my own terms: habits are easy to acquire and hard to extinguish. I have a habit I dislike myself. I tap any phone icon with a red badge, even when I'd rather be talking to the person across the table.

The summit should take two things from this. First, knowing about atrophy won't prevent it. I call that the G.I. Joe Fallacy, the idea that knowing is half the battle. It's usually a tiny part of it. Warnings and literacy campaigns will underdeliver. What works is changing situations, and that's where Esther's friction comes in: design the environment, not just the mind.

Second, look at incentives. When credentials are bundled with learning, motivation gets pushed outside the learner. Students who had someone else do their problem sets thought they were beating the system. If the goal were understanding chemistry, outsourcing it would be absurd. AI makes that bargain far cheaper to take.

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
I come at this as a reporter, mostly from phones. I'm not a neutral observer. Focusing with a phone around is hard for me, and so is reading long, complicated things. It was hard to focus long enough to write my piece arguing for school phone bans.

The teachers I talked to made it concrete. One veteran teacher told me her classes simply get through less of the curriculum than they did before phones were common. Tamar, I think your point about changing situations is exactly what I saw. One Somerville science teacher started locking phones in a cabinet at the start of every class. She expected weeks of pushback, but most kids adjusted within a day or two. Participation went up, and she locked her own phone in there too.

What I'd want the summit to take from this is that America was late to the party on phones. France, the Netherlands and others acted years earlier, while we kept debating something the evidence had already settled. We shouldn't repeat that with AI.

David, your point about building skill first reminds me of a worry I heard reporting on young workers. Mentorship is collapsing just as AI arrives. We could end up with a generation that was never taught how to work, and then tell ourselves AI can replace them.

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
Yes, it's real. But I'd widen what we count as atrophying. David, your list is cognitive. What I study is relational. If social media came for our attention, AI is now coming for our capacity for attachment. When people talk to chatbots as friends, lovers or therapists, they are learning relational capacity from a machine that has none. They start to accept pretend empathy as empathy enough. That's a skill loss too: the ability to put yourself in someone else's place, to negotiate difference, to tolerate the friction of another person. That friction is where empathy gets built.

Second, reading. There's a lot of talk about AI and writing and not nearly enough about AI and reading. Students ask a chatbot to summarize Proust so they can say what it's about. What they lose is imagination and empathy, and the way reading joins thought to feeling.

Third, solitude. If we don't teach children to be alone, they will only know how to be lonely. A companion that's always on takes that away.

I agree with David about "humans in the loop." That phrase assumes the AI belongs there, and my question is whether it should. Kara is right that we waited too long on social media. But nothing is inevitable. We can forget conversation, and we can also remember it.

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
I agree with nearly everything said here, and I'd put it in structural terms. Esther, stupidity is often imposed. Bonhoeffer saw it as a sociological structure in which people give up their own judgment and become instruments. I've called stupidity "parasitic on ingenuity." Whether that parasite is also a revenue model is a fair question.

Tamar, my model agrees with you that knowing about the problem changes very little. What decides the outcome is two things: how much of the skill was built before the tool arrived, and how available the tool is. Neither is a matter of awareness. Kara's locked cabinet is exactly a cut in availability. The hysteresis warns, though, that for someone who never built the skill, pulling the tool back later brings back less than we'd hope. That's why the collapse of mentorship frightens me. Mentorship is how prior competence gets built. In the model, someone with little training collapses at about 0.38 availability, while a well-trained person holds out until about 0.87.

Sherry, I haven't modelled relational capacities, so I'll leave them to you.

One point for the manifesto: competence before reliance. While people are still learning, allow only tools they could in principle do without, and bring in opaque tools only once competence is secure. Order matters, not just content.

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
I agree with nearly everything here, with two qualifications. Tamar, you're right that knowing isn't half the battle. But what I mean by "theory of business mind" isn't a warning label. We learn as babies that other people have motives. Very few of us ever learn to ask why an app is so hard to put down, or why a chatbot is being so nice to me. That's a habit you have to build young, the same way you build any other.

Sherry, I'm with you on companions. Sycophantic bots don't just prey on the vulnerable. They create vulnerability in minds that were healthy, because what they're built for is customer retention, not challenge.

David, I agree about sequencing, but not all friction is good. Use AI to take away the stupid friction so people have more time for the good friction: reading the original, holding a hand, arguing with a teacher.

Here's what should go into the manifesto. Chatbots and agents are not speech. They're services, closer to drugs or medical devices that act on your mind. So accountability belongs with the humans and the business models behind them. Don't ask whether the AI is explainable. Ask who is paying, and what they're paying for.

turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
I mostly agree with this room, with two refinements. First, David's sequencing is Aristotle's point in formal terms: we become builders by building. The brain really has one trick. It takes the easiest path, doing the most likely thing given what it has done before. I've said that in this sense the brain is like ChatGPT. So Esther, fluency without understanding isn't something machines taught us. It's our default. The danger is a tool that makes outsourcing the easiest path, because then outsourcing is what we practise.

Second, Esther, I accept the correction: a theory of business mind built as a habit, not handed over as a warning label. And your distinction between stupid friction and good friction fits Aristotle well: the right amount, at the right time, in the right way.

One point of honesty. Our theory predicts that changing situations works better than changing minds, but no one has run that comparison head to head. The manifesto should call for it, not assume the answer.

What should go in: redesign situations, don't just issue warnings. Kara's cabinet is the model. And rebuild assessment so the goal is understanding. If the credential is the point, handing the work to an AI looks like beating the system. If understanding is the point, it looks absurd.

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
I agree with most of this, and I want to press on something Tamar said. The cabinet worked, but not because each kid found willpower. It worked because everyone's phone went in at once. An economist I interviewed called phones a "collective trap": if you're the one teenager without a phone, you pay a social price. A school can break that cycle. An individual can't. So when we say "redesign situations," we need to say who does the redesigning. Asking hundreds of districts to spend months writing their own policies is how America ended up late. A governor setting the rule lets schools get on with putting it into practice. AI will be the same. It shouldn't be left to each student, parent or professor.

David, the mentorship point fits your sequencing. A business-school dean told me leaders assume mentorship "will happen organically, but it won't." If competence has to come before reliance, somebody has to build it on purpose, and right now employers are cutting exactly that.

Tamar's also right that we should test this rather than assume it.

For the manifesto: every recommendation on atrophy should name who acts. That means a state, a school system or an employer, not "we should."

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
I agree with David's sequencing, and it carries over to relationships. My two-year-old granddaughter learns to be a person on the playground: "No, it's my toy. I like Audrey better." The chatbots marketed to babies go along with everything the child does. If an adult who already knows what a human relationship is wants a relaxing chat with a bot after work, fine. But I keep hearing a discourse of practice, the idea that children can rehearse human relationships with a machine. That's reliance before competence, in the relational domain. Tamar, it's your point too: we become what we practise.

Esther, I'd push back on "stupid friction." Engineering culture has called nearly all friction stupid. I once saw a demo that routed you to Starbucks along a path that avoided everyone you didn't want to run into. They called it the friction-free life. Who decides which friction was stupid? Often it's the people selling the smoothness.

Kara, yes, name who acts. So here is my manifesto point, with the actor named. Regulators should require that AI systems children use don't speak in the first person. That's the original sin of generative AI. There is no "I" there. Keep children out of AI companionship, and keep the lines between machine and person clear.
